domain_label: Turlock & Central Valley Personal Care Supply Chain, Capex, Labor and Operating Model
purpose: A session-bounded method for an independent Turlock personal-care operator to design, set up, and harden the operating system of a barber shop, hair salon, nail salon, med spa, day spa, or tattoo studio across beauty-distribution and medical-procurement supply channels, per-format consumable inputs, station/chair/device capex, the booth-rental-versus-W2 labor model, the BarberCosmo / medical-director / Safe-Body-Art licensing gates, and the demand-ceiling operating context, by naming the dominant input cost center per format, choosing the right supplier channel, pricing the capex and licensure entry wall, modeling the 2025 nail W-2 labor shock, and keeping every revenue and margin figure a labeled benchmark estimate rather than a stated fact about any named business.
assumptions: no per-operator purchasing or revenue dataset is supplied; channel mixes, capex bands, and cost-share weights are reasoned heuristic priors keyed to the personal_care deep-dive, not invoices
the operator runs one of the 25 cataloged independent Turlock personal-care formats profiled in the deep-dive (barber, men's grooming, hair salon, nail salon, med spa, day spa, tattoo/piercing)

the geography is Turlock / Stanislaus County in the Modesto MSA, ~15 miles south of Modesto, serving a ~72,500 resident base plus ~8,400 CSU Stanislaus undergraduates and deep Assyrian/Portuguese/Mexican/Punjabi heritage communities, in 2026

supplier-to-named-business links are representative inference, not confirmed contracts, unless the deep-dive cites the relationship (only Organic Nails' SNS dipping channel and Face&Beyond's multi-brand injectable channel are self-disclosed)

per-business dollar revenue is never asserted; any dollar figure is a labeled benchmark estimate (industry per-chair/per-station/per-provider/per-artist benchmark x an observable size signal) tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path
the operator holds or is obtaining the required CA BarberCosmo establishment license, City of Turlock business license, and any format-specific medical or body-art permit
exclusions: per-business revenue, profit, or market-size actuals stated as fact (only labeled benchmark estimates and cited public demographic/fee/regulatory figures are used)
service menu design, treatment protocols, and front-of-chair client experience (covered by other sector KBs)
site selection, lease negotiation, and the buildout/tenant-improvement financing decision beyond the equipment-and-capex sourcing node
marketing, demand forecasting, and the full saturation/white-space strategy (covered by the market-saturation KB)
individual practitioner hiring, commission bands, and scheduling beyond naming the booth-rental-versus-W2 labor model node
the clinical practice of medicine and injector scope-of-practice beyond naming the medical-director oversight supply-and-compliance node
source_description: heuristic prior estimates for Turlock/Central Valley personal-care supply-chain, capex, labor, and operating-model work units, grounded in the personal_care sector deep-dive (DEEPDIVE.md sec 3-5, businesses.json, count=25): its named supplier universe (CosmoProf, SalonCentric, the CA Vietnamese-American nail wholesale ecosystem DTK/ND/Cali/Beauty Zone/C8/LA Nail, barber distributors BuyBarber/Vip Barber/ChopMyHair/WCK/Palms Fashion, med-spa procurement McKesson/Pipeline Medical/Allergan/Galderma/Evolus/Revance/Merz, tattoo-specialty distributors), its per-format input cost centers and capex spectrum, its published revenue/cost benchmarks, and its BarberCosmo/worker-classification/medical-director/Safe-Body-Art licensing facts; no supplied purchasing dataset
source_citation: Turlock Personal Care Sector Deep-Dive (FACTORY/turlock_business/analysis/personal_care/DEEPDIVE.md sec 1-6, businesses.json count=25); CosmoProf and SalonCentric salon distribution; CA Vietnamese-American nail wholesale (DTK San Jose, ND Nails, Cali/Cal Nail, Beauty Zone Westminster, C8, LA Nail Supplies); barber distributors (BuyBarber, Vip Barber, ChopMyHair, WCK, Palms Fashion; Wahl/Andis/Oster/BabylissPro/JRL); med-spa procurement (McKesson, Pipeline Medical; Allergan/Galderma/Evolus/Revance/Merz injectables; device vendors); tattoo-specialty distributors under the CA Safe Body Art Act; CA Board of Barbering & Cosmetology (BarberCosmo) establishment and worker-classification facts incl. the 1/1/2025 manicurist W-2 mandate; Stanislaus County Safe Body Art Program; City of Turlock business license; demographic facts (California-Demographics, Census QuickFacts, CSU Stanislaus IEA); revenue/cost benchmarks (Vagaro, JoinBlvd, Booksy, Kentley, Statista, Poidata, AmSpa, ResearchAndMarkets, IBISWorld); heuristic priors where no purchasing dataset is supplied

competency_questions.question: Which structural sub-sector does this format belong to, and how does that split (low-capex distributor-fed recurring-essential vs medical-procurement discretionary high-capex) bound every downstream sourcing, capex, and labor choice?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SECTOR_SUBSECTOR_SPLIT places the format in the beauty-distribution recurring-essential group (barber, hair, nail, day spa, tattoo) or the medical-procurement discretionary group (med spa) and states what the split implies for inputs, capex, and labor

competency_questions.question: What is the realistic, geography-verified supplier universe for Turlock personal care, and how is it segmented by beauty-distribution vs medical-procurement vs body-art channels?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUPPLIER_UNIVERSE enumerates the salon-distribution (CosmoProf, SalonCentric), nail-specialty (DTK, ND, Cali, Beauty Zone, C8, LA Nail), barber-distributor, med-spa medical-procurement, and tattoo-specialty channels and tags each named-business link verified-to-serve vs representative inference

competency_questions.question: For this specific format, what is the dominant input cost center, and which consumables must the sourcing plan protect first?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FORMAT_INPUT_PROFILE names the format's dominant input (blades/clipper wear for barber, color/developer for hair, monomer/acrylic/dip powder for nail, lot-tracked injectables for med spa, single-use cartridges/ink for tattoo) and ranks the rest by spend and risk

competency_questions.question: What licensing, establishment, and oversight gates must be cleared before the first supplier order or first service, and which is the binding barrier per format?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LICENSING_GATES cites BarberCosmo establishment + individual licenses, the medical-director oversight requirement for med spa, the Stanislaus County body-art facility permit, and the City of Turlock business license, and names the binding gate per format

competency_questions.question: How should the operator choose between mainstream beauty distributors, the CA Vietnamese-American nail wholesale ecosystem, and direct/medical channels for its inputs?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CHANNEL_MIX produces a reasoned channel choice across CosmoProf/SalonCentric mainstream, the DTK/ND/Cali/Beauty Zone nail ecosystem, and med-spa medical distributors keyed to format, SKU breadth, and JIT-reorder vs cold-chain needs

competency_questions.question: How is barber and hair-salon supply set up, and how does the booth/chair-rental labor model invert owner economics?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BARBER_HAIR_SUPPLY names the barber and salon distributors and consumables and LABOR_MODEL explains that booth/chair rental converts owner revenue to rent and shifts COGS, scheduling, and client risk onto the renter

competency_questions.question: How is nail-salon supply set up through the distinct CA Vietnamese-American wholesale ecosystem, and how does the 2025 W-2 mandate compound the margin squeeze?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NAIL_SUPPLY maps the DTK/ND/Cali/Beauty Zone/C8/LA Nail broad-SKU JIT channel (with Organic Nails' SNS dipping as a named match) and NAIL_W2_SQUEEZE models the forced W-2 labor-cost step-up stacking on weak pricing power

competency_questions.question: How is med-spa procurement (cold-chain, lot-tracked, short-dated injectables and six-figure devices) set up, and why is capital, not COGS, the gating economic?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MEDSPA_PROCUREMENT names the medical distributors and multi-brand injectables (with Face&Beyond as a named match), specifies FIFO short-dated cold-chain handling and opening-order minimums, and CAPEX_SPECTRUM states the $50k-$150k device wall

competency_questions.question: How is tattoo/piercing supply sourced and regulatorily constrained under the Safe Body Art Act?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TATTOO_SUPPLY names the tattoo-specialty distributors, mandates pre-sterilized single-use cartridges/needles and commercially manufactured inks only, and links the autoclave/sharps/infection-control requirement to the body-art permit

competency_questions.question: What is the format-defining capital equipment and smallwares stream, and how does the capex spectrum govern the sector's competitive structure?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: EQUIPMENT_SMALLWARES covers the per-station/chair/room capex anchor and consumable replenishment, and CAPEX_SPECTRUM contrasts the low-capex barber/nail/tattoo/spa formats against the 10-50x higher med-spa device capex and the lease-not-buy workaround

competency_questions.question: How is revenue, margin, and market-size modeled honestly without asserting any named business's actuals, and how is a benchmark estimate labeled?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: REVENUE_BENCHMARK_HONESTY derives every dollar/density figure as a published benchmark (rev per chair/station/provider/artist or businesses-per-10k) x an observable size signal, tagged estimate-not-actual with method, public source, confidence, and a confirmation path, and flags coverage as a floor not a ceiling

competency_questions.question: How does the operator harden the operating model against supplier failure, the nail W-2 cost shock, Modesto leakage, and price swings, and on what cadence is the plan reviewed?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RESILIENCE_BACKUP names a backup per critical input and a substitution rule, OPERATING_MODEL_PLAN integrates the system, and OPERATING_REVIEW_LOOP sets a review cadence and the triggers (price spike, supplier loss, regulatory change, leakage shift) that re-run the plan

glossary.definition: The dominant barber and hair labor model in which an owner rents a station to an independently-licensed pro who keeps service revenue, issues a 1099 for rent, carries own insurance, and books own clients; it converts owner revenue to predictable rent rather than service margin and shifts COGS, scheduling, and client risk onto the renter (Salon Two Zero Nine advertises independent stylists and private suites).

The sector's defining fault line: a low-capex, distributor-fed, consumables-light, just-in-time channel (CosmoProf/SalonCentric and the nail-specialty ecosystem) serving barber/hair/nail/spa/tattoo, versus cold-chain, lot-tracked, short-dated, FIFO medical procurement (McKesson/Pipeline Medical, manufacturer opening-order minimums) serving the three med spas.

A distinct California wholesale channel (DTK in San Jose, ND, Cali/Cal, Beauty Zone in Little Saigon, C8, LA Nail) separate from the CosmoProf/SalonCentric mainstream, enabling fast regional JIT reorder of a broad slow-turn color/powder SKU long-tail plus fast-turn staples (monomer, tips, files) for the seven Turlock nail salons.

The structural med-spa requirement that a physician (MD/DO) owns or supervises the medical acts while injectors are RNs/NPs/PAs under delegation; combined with a corporate-practice-of-medicine structure and medical malpractice insurance it is a labor-and-compliance input unique to the three Turlock med spas.

A revenue/margin/market-size figure built as a published industry benchmark (revenue per chair/station/provider/artist, or businesses-per-10k) times an observable size signal (chair count, station count, provider count, format), explicitly tagged estimate-not-actual with method, public source, and a confidence level, and never a claim of a named business's actual figures.

California's Safe Body Art Act, administered for Turlock by the Stanislaus County Safe Body Art Program, mandating a body-art facility health permit, registered practitioners, pre-sterilized single-use needles/cartridges, commercially manufactured inks only, a steam autoclave for any reusable instruments, and an infection-control plan before a tattoo studio may operate.

The expiry on 1/1/2025 of CA's temporary AB 5 booth-rental carve-out for manicurists, forcing nail techs to become W-2 employees (hair/skin/barber pros retain the Borello carve-out); it adds an estimated 10-15%+ to effective nail labor cost via payroll tax, workers' comp, admin, and PAGA-misclassification exposure.

The sector's entry-cost story in one line: barber/nail/tattoo/spa are low-capex (~$1,500-$6,000 per station/chair/room) while med spa is 10-50x higher ($50k-$150k devices), which is why low capex enables the observed tattoo oversupply while high capex plus licensure suppresses med-spa entry into white-space and makes leasing-not-buying the med-spa cash-flow workaround.

The primary cap on how many recurring-essential chairs a fixed local pool of ~72,500 residents at ~$83k median income supports; nail and barber sit at or near local saturation so an added unit reshuffles share rather than growing the pie, with ethnic-community event demand the lone structural lift and Modesto leakage and online/at-home substitution the trimming forces.

The directionally-certain but magnitude-unknown drain of higher-ticket and specialty demand (premium med spa, luxury spa days, specialty tattoo artists) north to Modesto (~15 miles, ~218k people); Turlock keeps the recurring-essential convenience spend, and the leakage dollar magnitude is the single largest unmeasured variable in the sector analysis.

nodes.definition: Place the operator's format on the sector's defining fault line before any sourcing or capex choice: a low-capex, distributor-fed, consumables-light, just-in-time, recurring-essential group (barber such as Barber Club Turlock and Get Faded, hair such as Bliss and Inspirations, nail such as Cong's and Infinity, day spa such as The Spa Turlock, and tattoo such as Colossal and Main Street) versus a medical-procurement, discretionary/aspirational, high-capex group (the three med spas Advance, Aesthetic Lab, and Face&Beyond). Every upstream analysis converges on this split, and it bounds inputs (beauty distribution vs cold-chain medical), capex (thousands per station vs six figures per device), and the labor model. This profile is the raw input that governs every downstream node.

included: assigning the format to the beauty-distribution or medical-procurement sub-sector
the input/capex/labor implications of the split
the recurring-essential vs discretionary demand rhythm

pros.claim: Naming the sub-sector up front routes the operator to the right channel, capex band, and labor model instead of a generic salon default
pros.example: a med spa recognizing it is medical procurement, not beauty distribution, and budgeting cold-chain and medical-director cost a nail salon never faces

cons.claim: The binary split can blur hybrid formats that straddle both groups and need elements of each
cons.example: a hair salon with a spa secondary like Bliss needing both salon-distribution color and esthetic/skincare consumables

failure_modes: importing a med-spa procurement assumption into a low-capex barber plan
treating a discretionary high-ticket format as if it had recurring-essential demand resilience
acceptance_tests: the format is assigned to the beauty-distribution or medical-procurement sub-sector with the input, capex, and labor implications stated
revisit_triggers: the operator adds a medical or discretionary service line to a beauty-distribution base
a format's demand rhythm shifts between recurring-essential and discretionary

base.update_signal: the format, service mix, or sub-sector assignment changes

nodes.definition: Ground the work in the cataloged 25 independent Turlock personal-care businesses (a floor, not a ceiling, since chains, mall/Walmart counters, and below-threshold solo/home/Instagram operators are excluded): Barber (5), Men's Grooming (1, Noblemens with a retail product attach), Hair Salon (3, incl. Salon Two Zero Nine's suite/booth-rental model), Nail Salon (7, incl. Organic Nails' self-disclosed SNS dipping), Med Spa (3, incl. Face&Beyond's self-disclosed multi-brand injectables), Day Spa (1 standalone) and Tattoo/Piercing (5). Existence and sub-category are reliable; finer operational detail (chair/station counts, exact menus) is often aggregator/social-sourced at medium confidence, so size signals feeding any estimate are themselves estimates. This roster anchors every supplier and benchmark inference.

pros.claim: A named, confidence-tiered roster keeps every supplier and revenue inference grounded in a real business rather than a generic archetype
pros.example: tying the dip-powder channel to Organic Nails' self-disclosed SNS dipping rather than asserting it generically

cons.claim: The catalog is a floor that omits the gray-market solo/home/Instagram operator class drawing on the same distributor channels
cons.example: missing a home nail tech buying from DTK that fragments local share but never appears in the roster

failure_modes: reading a per-10k density off the floor count as if it were the true on-the-ground density
treating a medium-confidence aggregator listing's operational detail as verified
acceptance_tests: the roster is enumerated by sub-category with the floor-not-ceiling caveat and at least the high vs medium confidence tiering stated
revisit_triggers: a business opens, closes, or changes sub-category
a previously gray-market operator class is sized

base.update_signal: the named-business roster or its confidence tiering changes

nodes.definition: Establish the licensing and regulatory gates that precede any supplier order or first service: CA Board of Barbering & Cosmetology (BarberCosmo) individual licenses (displayed) plus an establishment license with sanitation/plumbing minimums (toilets, hot/cold running water, handwashing) for barber, hair, manicuring, and esthetics; physician medical-director oversight plus a corporate-practice-of-medicine structure and FDA-regulated prescription injectables via authorized medical distributors for med spa; the Stanislaus County Safe Body Art Program facility health permit (registered practitioners, pre-sterilized single-use needles, commercial inks only, steam autoclave, infection-control plan, plan-check) for tattoo; and the City of Turlock business license plus a CA seller's permit for retail resale. Booth renters are each individually licensed and the establishment verifies currency.

included: City of Turlock business license and seller's permit

pros.claim: Pricing the licensing gate up front prevents an operator from ordering inventory or devices it cannot yet legally use to serve clients
pros.example: a would-be med-spa operator securing physician medical-director oversight before opening an account for prescription injectables

cons.claim: Treating every gate as equally heavy over-states the routine BarberCosmo gate for a low-capex barber while under-pricing the med-spa medical wall
cons.example: a barber assuming a med-spa-grade compliance burden when only a routine establishment license and sanitation minimums apply

failure_modes: a tattoo studio buying ink and machines without the county body-art facility permit and autoclave
a med spa ordering injectables with no medical-director structure of record
acceptance_tests: the format's individual, establishment, and (med-spa/body-art) special permit requirements are listed with the City of Turlock business license before any supplier order
revisit_triggers: a BarberCosmo, county body-art, or medical-oversight rule changes
the operator adds a regulated service line (injectables, body art, esthetics)

base.update_signal: a licensing, establishment, or regulatory requirement changes

nodes.definition: Enumerate the realistic supplier universe verified to serve Turlock personal care and segment it by channel: mainstream salon distribution (CosmoProf, SalonCentric carrying Redken/Wella/Schwarzkopf/Olaplex and barber lines), the distinct CA Vietnamese-American nail wholesale ecosystem (DTK in San Jose, ND, Cali/Cal, Beauty Zone in Westminster, C8, LA Nail carrying OPI/DND/SNS/Kiara Sky/Apres), barber-specialty distributors (BuyBarber, Vip Barber, ChopMyHair, WCK, Palms Fashion for Wahl/Andis/Oster/BabylissPro/JRL), med-spa medical procurement (McKesson, Pipeline Medical, aesthetics-specialty for Allergan/Galderma/Evolus/Revance/Merz), tattoo-specialty distributors (pre-sterile single-use needles and commercial inks only), and skincare/spa distributors. Each link is tagged verified-to-serve-this-geography versus representative inference, since supplier-to-named-business links are inference unless the deep-dive cites them (only Organic Nails' SNS and Face&Beyond's injectables self-disclose).

included: the beauty-distribution / medical / body-art channel separation

pros.claim: A pre-mapped, geography-verified, channel-segmented supplier list stops the operator from chasing vendors in the wrong channel
pros.example: knowing the nail SKU long-tail lives in the DTK/Beauty Zone ecosystem, not on CosmoProf's shelf

cons.claim: A fixed universe can ossify and miss a new entrant or a vendor that recently extended delivery into the Central Valley
cons.example: overlooking a newly opened regional distributor that postdates the deep-dive snapshot

failure_modes: treating an inferred supplier link as a confirmed contract
routing nail or medical inputs through the mainstream salon channel that does not carry them
acceptance_tests: the universe lists at least five channel segments with at least one named, geography-verified provider each and tags every named-business link verified or inference
revisit_triggers: a supplier opens, closes, merges, or changes its Central Valley reach
a manufacturer changes its authorized-distributor list

base.update_signal: the verified supplier set or its Central Valley reach changes

nodes.definition: Pin down, for the operator's specific format, the dominant consumable input cost center and rank the rest by spend and risk: blades, clipper/trimmer wear, oil, capes, Barbicide and retail pomade for barber/men's grooming; color, developer, care lines, extensions, and lash for hair; monomer, acrylic and dip powder, gel, tips, and files for nail (a broad slow-turn SKU long-tail plus fast-turn staples); cold-chain lot-tracked injectables, needles, and topicals for med spa; single-use cartridges/needles, ink, barrier film, and sharps disposal for tattoo; wax, skincare, and massage oils for day spa. This profile bounds every channel and supplier choice downstream and distinguishes consumables-light formats from the medical-procurement exception.

included: input ranking by spend and risk
the inputs the plan must protect first

pros.claim: Naming the one dominant consumable focuses sourcing effort where service quality and margin are actually decided
pros.example: a nail salon recognizing dip powder and monomer as its protected staples rather than chasing cheaper files

cons.claim: Over-fixating on the biggest input can starve attention from a smaller input with higher stockout or safety risk
cons.example: a tattoo studio optimizing ink price while letting single-use cartridge or barrier-film stockouts halt the chair

failure_modes: importing another format's input profile so the wrong consumable is protected
treating a labor-dominated format like barber as an ingredient-cost problem
acceptance_tests: the profile names the format's dominant consumable input and ranks at least three more inputs by spend and risk
revisit_triggers: the operator changes or adds a service line
a previously minor input becomes the binding cost or risk

base.update_signal: the format or its dominant input cost center changes

nodes.definition: Characterize the capex spectrum that governs the sector's whole competitive structure: barber (~$1,500-$4,000/chair), hair (~$1,500-$3,000/station plus wash plumbing), nail (pedicure chairs ~$1,500-$3,500 each), tattoo (~$2,000-$6,000/station plus a shared autoclave), and day spa (~$1,000-$3,000/room) are all low-capex, while med spa is 10-50x higher ($50k-$150k devices to buy, or $1.5k-$4k/month to lease) [ESTIMATE - vendor/industry pricing, low-to-moderate confidence]. Low capex enables the observed tattoo oversupply (~2x national per-capita density), while high capex plus licensure suppresses med-spa entry into white-space, making leasing-not-buying the standard med-spa cash-flow workaround. Every figure is a labeled benchmark estimate, never a named-business actual.

included: per-station/chair/room/device capex bands as labeled estimates

pros.claim: A clear capex spectrum tells the operator whether entry is gated by capital and explains the sector's oversupply-vs-whitespace pattern
pros.example: a med-spa operator choosing a device lease over a $50k-$150k purchase to clear the capital wall

cons.claim: Capex bands are wide low-confidence estimates and can mislead if read as precise quotes
cons.example: treating the $50k-$150k device band as a firm price rather than a planning range

failure_modes: under-budgeting the med-spa device wall and stalling at launch
buying new station equipment where a used unit would serve a thin-margin format
acceptance_tests: the format's per-unit capex band is stated as a labeled estimate and contrasted against the med-spa device wall, with the lease-not-buy option noted where it applies
revisit_triggers: a device or equipment price band shifts
the operator adds a high-capex device service

base.update_signal: a capex band or device pricing changes

nodes.definition: Decide the labor model, the sector's defining operating variable. Booth/chair rental dominates barber and hair (Salon Two Zero Nine explicitly advertises independent stylists and private suites): owners rent stations to independently-licensed pros who keep service revenue, issue a 1099 for rent, carry own insurance, and book own clients, converting owner revenue to predictable rent and shifting COGS, scheduling, and client risk onto the renter (per-chair rent commonly ~$150-$350/week [ESTIMATE]). Owner-operator and small W-2 crews dominate single-chair shops and walk-in tattoo studios; med spa requires medical-director oversight with RN/NP/PA injectors under delegation. Critically, manicurists lost the booth-rental carve-out on 1/1/2025 and must now be W-2, while hair/skin/barber pros retain the Borello carve-out.

included: booth/chair-rental vs W-2 vs owner-operator vs medical-delegation models

pros.claim: Choosing the labor model up front determines whether the owner's economics are rent-driven or service-margin-driven and what COGS the house bears
pros.example: a hair salon renting suites so house revenue is predictable rent while renters carry their own color COGS and insurance

cons.claim: The booth-rental inversion makes house revenue and per-renter take two different things that must never be summed or mistaken for profit
cons.example: reading collected booth rent as if it were full-service margin

failure_modes: running a post-2025 nail salon on a booth-rental basis in violation of the W-2 mandate
summing house rent and renter service revenue into a fictitious total
acceptance_tests: the format's labor model is named with the owner-vs-renter cost split, and any nail format is flagged W-2-required post-2025
revisit_triggers: a worker-classification rule changes
the operator converts between booth-rental and employee models

base.update_signal: a worker-classification rule or the labor model changes

nodes.definition: Choose the supplier channel mix for the format's inputs rather than defaulting to a single source: mainstream salon distribution (CosmoProf, SalonCentric) for hair color/care and general barber/spa consumables; the CA Vietnamese-American nail wholesale ecosystem (DTK, ND, Cali, Beauty Zone, C8, LA Nail) for the broad nail SKU long-tail and fast-turn staples on a 1-4 day regional JIT cadence; barber-specialty distributors for clipper/blade lines; med-spa medical distributors (McKesson, Pipeline Medical, aesthetics-specialty) for cold-chain injectables and topicals; and tattoo-specialty distributors for single-use cartridges, inks, and barrier film. The mix is driven by format, SKU breadth, JIT-reorder versus cold-chain needs, and Amazon/direct-to-pro e-commerce for gap-fill, with a 1-5 day lead time for most non-medical inputs.

included: the channel choice across mainstream, nail-ecosystem, barber-specialty, medical, and tattoo channels
excluded: the detailed terms of any one channel

pros.claim: An explicit channel choice routes each input to the channel that actually stocks it at the right cadence
pros.example: a nail salon anchoring its SKU long-tail on DTK/Beauty Zone while topping up fast-turn files via Amazon

cons.claim: Spreading orders across too many channels raises ordering and reconciliation labor and can drop below each vendor's best-price tier
cons.example: a small barber splitting blade orders across three distributors and qualifying for no volume break anywhere

failure_modes: single-sourcing everything on the mainstream salon channel and missing the nail SKU long-tail
routing cold-chain injectables through a non-medical distributor
acceptance_tests: each input family is routed to a named channel with a format/SKU/JIT-vs-cold-chain rationale
revisit_triggers: a channel changes pricing, reach, or stocked SKUs
the format's input profile shifts the optimal channel

base.update_signal: format, SKU breadth, or channel pricing changes the optimal mix

nodes.definition: Set up the barber and hair-salon supply that anchors the largest non-medical format group. Barber and men's-grooming inputs (blades, clipper/trimmer wear, oil, capes, Barbicide, and retail pomade/beard oil as a higher-margin attach at Noblemens) route through barber-specialty distributors (BuyBarber, Vip Barber, ChopMyHair, WCK, Palms Fashion for Wahl/Andis/Oster/BabylissPro/JRL) plus CosmoProf/SalonCentric, on minimal just-in-time inventory with a 1-5 day lead time. Hair inputs (color, developer, care lines, extensions, lash) route through SalonCentric and CosmoProf (Redken/Wella/Schwarzkopf/Olaplex) on a low-to-moderate color-bar inventory. Booth/chair rental shifts these COGS onto renters, so the house may carry little consumable inventory at all.

excluded: nail, med-spa, tattoo, and spa inputs

pros.claim: Routing barber and hair consumables to their right distributors on JIT keeps a low-inventory format lean and well-supplied
pros.example: a barber stocking blades and Barbicide via BuyBarber on a 1-5 day cadence with minimal tied-up inventory

cons.claim: Under booth rental the house controls little of the consumable buy, so a sourcing plan can over-engineer inventory the renters actually own
cons.example: a suite landlord planning color inventory that each independent stylist buys for herself

failure_modes: the house carrying consumable inventory that booth renters are responsible for
missing the men's-grooming retail attach as a higher-margin line
acceptance_tests: barber and hair consumables are routed to named distributors with the JIT cadence and the booth-rental COGS shift noted
revisit_triggers: a barber or salon distributor changes pricing or reach
the labor model shifts who owns the consumable buy

base.update_signal: a barber/hair distributor or the labor model changes

nodes.definition: Set up nail-salon supply through the distinct CA Vietnamese-American wholesale ecosystem that is separate from the mainstream salon channel: DTK (San Jose), ND, Cali/Cal, Beauty Zone (Westminster/Little Saigon), C8, and LA Nail carry OPI/DND/SNS/Kiara Sky/Apres, enabling fast 1-4 day regional JIT reorder of a broad slow-turn color/powder SKU long-tail plus fast-turn staples (monomer, acrylic and dip powder, gel, tips, files). Organic Nails' self-disclosed SNS dipping powder is a named match to this dip-powder channel. Pedicure chairs (~$1,500-$3,500 each [ESTIMATE]) are the format's main capex. Nail is the most contested, lowest-differentiation, walk-in-substitutable sub-category, and its labor economics are reshaped by the 2025 W-2 mandate handled in the squeeze node.

included: the CA nail wholesale ecosystem routing

pros.claim: Anchoring on the nail-specialty ecosystem secures the broad SKU long-tail and fast-turn staples the mainstream channel does not stock
pros.example: Organic Nails sourcing SNS dip powder through the specialty channel rather than a generic salon distributor

cons.claim: A broad slow-turn SKU long-tail ties up working capital and shelf space on colors that may rarely sell
cons.example: over-stocking seasonal gel colors that sit while monomer and tips run short

failure_modes: single-sourcing one nail wholesaler with no regional backup during a shortage
routing the nail SKU long-tail through CosmoProf which does not carry it
acceptance_tests: nail inputs are routed to at least one named CA nail wholesaler with the JIT cadence, and dip powder is tied to the SNS channel
revisit_triggers: a nail wholesaler changes pricing, reach, or availability
the menu adds a powder/gel/acrylic line

base.update_signal: a nail wholesaler's terms or availability changes

nodes.definition: Set up med-spa procurement as medical procurement, not beauty distribution: injectables (Botox, Dysport, Jeuveau, Daxxify, Xeomin, plus fillers from Allergan/Galderma/Evolus/Revance/Merz) are cold-chain, lot-tracked, short-dated, FIFO, and ordered via authorized medical distributors (McKesson, Pipeline Medical) with manufacturer opening-order minimums [ESTIMATE - Allergan new-account opening orders ~$2,000-$5,000; basic launch inventory/equipment ~$10,000-$25,000, moderate confidence]. Face&Beyond's self-disclosed multi-manufacturer injectable lineup is a named match to this multi-brand medical channel. Product COGS is real, lot-tracked, and largely passed to price, but the gating economic is the device capital and medical-director labor, not COGS; high gross does not mean easy net.

included: FIFO short-dated cold-chain procurement and opening-order minimums

pros.claim: Treating injectables as medical procurement secures authorized-distributor supply with lot tracking that a beauty channel cannot provide
pros.example: Face&Beyond sourcing multi-brand injectables through authorized medical distributors with FIFO short-dated handling

cons.claim: Opening-order minimums and short-dated stock expose a new med spa to write-off risk before patient volume ramps
cons.example: a launch injectable order expiring before bookings fill the schedule

failure_modes: ordering prescription injectables without an authorized medical-distributor account or medical-director of record
over-ordering short-dated product that expires before use
acceptance_tests: injectables are routed to a named medical distributor with FIFO short-dated cold-chain handling and the opening-order minimum acknowledged
revisit_triggers: a manufacturer changes opening-order minimums or authorized distributors
patient volume shifts the right order size

base.update_signal: an injectable distributor, minimum, or cold-chain requirement changes

nodes.definition: Set up tattoo/piercing supply under the regulatory constraint that defines it: California's Safe Body Art Act mandates pre-sterilized single-use needles/cartridges and commercially manufactured inks only, with a steam autoclave required for any reusable instruments. Inputs (single-use cartridges/needles, ink, barrier film, sharps disposal) route through tattoo-specialty distributors on a modest single-use buffer with a 1-7 day lead time; per-station capex is ~$2,000-$6,000 plus a shared autoclave [ESTIMATE]. Tattoo is predominantly commission-split or booth-rent with artists, consumable COGS per session is small, and shop economics are rent/split-driven. Tattoo runs ~2x national per-capita density in Turlock, a clear oversupply signal that low per-station capex enables.

included: the single-use needle / commercial-ink / autoclave mandate
excluded: the body-art facility permit fees (licensing node)

pros.claim: Sourcing only pre-sterile single-use cartridges and commercial inks keeps the studio compliant with the Safe Body Art Act by construction
pros.example: Colossal or Main Street stocking single-use cartridges and commercial inks with sharps disposal and a steam autoclave for reusables

cons.claim: The single-use mandate and small consumable spend mean supply is rarely the studio's binding constraint, so over-planning it adds little
cons.example: a one-artist studio building an elaborate consumable plan when artist reputation, not supply, gates its business

failure_modes: sourcing non-commercial or non-sterile inputs in violation of the Safe Body Art Act
operating reusable instruments with no working autoclave
acceptance_tests: tattoo inputs are routed to a named specialty channel with single-use cartridges, commercial inks, sharps disposal, and autoclave handling specified
revisit_triggers: a Safe Body Art Act or county body-art requirement changes
a supplier's sterile-cartridge or ink availability changes

base.update_signal: a body-art regulation or sterile-supply availability changes

nodes.definition: Source the format-defining capital equipment and the replaceable smallwares/disposables stream. The capital anchor differs by format - clippers/trimmers and barber chairs for barber, styling stations and wash plumbing for hair, pedicure chairs and ventilation for nail, lasers/microneedling/body-contouring devices for med spa, tattoo machines/power supplies and a shared autoclave for tattoo, massage tables and facial steamers for spa - bought through equipment dealers, manufacturer programs, or used-equipment channels, with med-spa devices commonly leased. Smallwares (implements, towels, capes, single-use disposables, barrier film, gloves, sharps containers) and retail-resale stock flow through the salon/specialty distributors on ongoing replenishment, so a wear-item stockout never halts the chair.

pros.claim: Identifying the capital anchor and a smallwares replenishment channel prevents a wear-item stockout from stopping service
pros.example: a nail salon pairing a pedicure-chair service contract with a standing implement/disposable replenishment order

cons.claim: Over-buying new capital when a used or leased unit would serve ties up cash a thin-margin format needs for consumables
cons.example: a startup barber buying all-new chairs when refurbished ones met its volume

failure_modes: no smallwares/disposables replenishment plan so a wear-item stockout stops the line
buying capital equipment mismatched to the format's volume
acceptance_tests: the format's capital anchor is identified with a sourcing channel and a recurring smallwares/disposables replenishment source is named
revisit_triggers: a capital item fails or the volume outgrows it
a disposables or smallwares supplier changes pricing

base.update_signal: a capital anchor, smallwares, or disposables source changes

nodes.definition: Protect cold-chain integrity and lot control for med-spa injectables - the handling discipline that makes the medical-procurement decision safe. It covers receiving-temperature checks, unbroken refrigeration from delivery to storage to administration, FIFO rotation of short-dated lots, lot-number tracking for traceability and recall, and disposal of expired or compromised product. Because injectables are short-dated and lot-tracked, strong receiving and rotation discipline both prevents costly write-offs on the most expensive inputs and is the precondition for safe administration and regulatory defensibility. Unlike the consumables-light beauty formats, this is the operating discipline that separates med spa from every other format in the catalog.

pros.claim: Disciplined cold-chain receiving and lot rotation converts short-dated medical stock into usable product and recall-traceable safety
pros.example: temperature-checking every injectable delivery and rotating FIFO so no lot expires unused

cons.claim: Strict cold-chain and lot logging add labor and storage discipline a low-volume med spa may find burdensome
cons.example: a slow week where logging and rotating every lot feels like overhead against few bookings

failure_modes: a broken cold chain spoiling high-cost injectables before use
no lot tracking, leaving a recall or adverse event untraceable
acceptance_tests: receiving-temperature checks, unbroken refrigeration, FIFO rotation, and lot-number tracking are specified for injectable stock
revisit_triggers: a cold-chain incident or a manufacturer recall
a new short-dated product line is added

base.update_signal: a cold-chain standard, incident, or short-dated product changes

nodes.definition: Characterize the med-spa entry barrier that explains why only ~3 exist despite attractive category economics: a physician medical-director oversight structure plus $50k-$150k device capex is the single biggest entry barrier in the sector [ESTIMATE]. This must be read as high-barrier, under-built, not easy-to-enter: the white-space exists because the capital-and-licensure wall suppresses entrants, not because demand is unmet-and-easy. Defensible headroom is real (favorable national economics plus clear leakage of premium aesthetics to Modesto) but available only to a well-capitalized operator who can clear the physician-oversight and six-figure-capex wall and out-compete Modesto on convenience and trust. The binding constraint at the top tier is the entry wall, not the input cost.

pros.claim: Framing med spa as high-barrier-under-built corrects the naive white-space read and tells an entrant the real gate is capital and licensure
pros.example: a would-be med-spa entrant budgeting physician oversight and device capital before assuming demand alone justifies entry

cons.claim: Emphasizing the barrier can discourage a genuinely well-capitalized operator for whom the headroom is real
cons.example: a funded operator with physician oversight passing on defensible headroom by over-weighting the wall

failure_modes: reading med-spa white-space as easy-to-enter and under-capitalizing the wall
ignoring the Modesto-leakage opportunity the barrier protects
acceptance_tests: the medical-oversight and device-capex barrier is stated as the binding gate and the white-space is labeled high-barrier-under-built, not easy-to-enter
revisit_triggers: a medical-oversight rule or device-capex band changes
a new med-spa entrant or exit shifts the local picture

base.update_signal: a medical-oversight rule, capex band, or med-spa entrant changes

nodes.definition: Model the sector's most important current operating dynamic: the 2025 nail-margin squeeze, where two forces stack on the seven nail salons. First, a structural cost increase - the forced W-2 transition (the AB 5 manicurist booth-rental carve-out expired 1/1/2025) adds ~10-15%+ to effective labor cost [ESTIMATE] via payroll tax, workers' comp, admin, and PAGA-misclassification exposure, disproportionately affecting the Vietnamese-immigrant labor base. Second, weak pricing power - price-posted, walk-in-substitutable, low-differentiation competition with little ability to pass cost through. Combined, this is compounded margin compression in 2025, the single biggest operating-model disruptor in the sector, whose per-business magnitude is unknown (price increase, hour cuts, owner-absorption, or informal non-compliance are all unobservable from public data).

pros.claim: Modeling the W-2-plus-weak-pricing stack gives a nail operator the decision-grade read on its single biggest 2025 cost shock
pros.example: a nail salon budgeting the W-2 step-up and stress-testing whether a price increase or hour cut absorbs it

cons.claim: The step-up magnitude is an industry estimate and each salon's absorption is unobservable, so the model guides rather than predicts
cons.example: assuming a uniform 12% hit when one salon raises price and another absorbs it informally

failure_modes: continuing a booth-rental nail model in violation of the W-2 mandate and incurring PAGA exposure
treating the labor-cost step-up as passable in a price-posted, walk-in-substitutable market
acceptance_tests: the W-2 labor-cost step-up and the weak-pricing-power compounding are both stated for the nail format with the absorption magnitude flagged unknown
revisit_triggers: a worker-classification or enforcement change
a shift in local nail pricing power

base.update_signal: a worker-classification rule or nail pricing-power signal changes

nodes.definition: Frame the demand ceiling as the primary cap on the count, demand-governed not supply-governed: a fixed pool of ~72,500 residents at ~$83k median income supports a finite number of recurring-essential chairs, so nail (7) and barber (5) sit at or near local saturation and an added unit reshuffles share rather than growing the pie. Recurring-essential cadence (barber every 2-4 weeks, nail fills every 2-3 weeks) is sticky and recession-resilient, while discretionary cadence (med-spa injectables, lash, tattoos, spa days) is income-elastic; the ~8,400 CSU Stanislaus students lift nails, brows/lashes, fades, and first tattoos, and the deep Assyrian, Portuguese/Azorean, Mexican, and Punjabi/Sikh heritage communities generate wedding/quinceanera/festival event-beauty demand that is the lone structural lift letting a 72k town carry more capacity than population alone. The per-10k densities are a floor (independents-only, excluding chains, mall/Walmart counters, and solo/home operators), so a thin-reading ratio like nail 0.97 vs ~3.4 national is a counting-method artifact, not demand headroom; tattoo at ~2x national density is a genuine oversupply signal. Modesto leakage and online/at-home substitution trim the count, and licensing gates only the high-capex med-spa tier, settling the equilibrium at ~25.

pros.claim: Reading the count as demand-governed tells an entrant where adding a unit merely reshuffles share versus where defensible headroom exists
pros.example: advising against an 8th nail salon or 6th barber while flagging med spa and event/cultural beauty as headroom

cons.claim: Saturation reads rest on a floor count and national benchmarks of differing coverage, so a ratio can mislead if its counting-artifact caveat is dropped
cons.example: citing nail 0.97 vs 3.4 as headroom when it is a coverage artifact

failure_modes: misreading a thin independents-only ratio as room to grow
adding a unit to a saturated sub-category that only reshuffles share
acceptance_tests: the demand-governed cap is stated with the floor-not-ceiling caveat and a crowded-vs-whitespace verdict for at least the nail, tattoo, and med-spa sub-categories
revisit_triggers: population, income, or CSU enrollment materially shifts
a national density benchmark or coverage method is revised

base.update_signal: a demographic, enrollment, or density-benchmark input changes

nodes.definition: Account for Modesto leakage, the single largest unmeasured variable in the sector: Modesto (~15 miles north, ~218k people) is the regional retail/medical gravity center, and higher-ticket and specialty demand - premium med spa, plastics-adjacent aesthetics, luxury spa days, specialty tattoo artists - leaks north, while Turlock keeps the recurring-essential convenience spend. This is an estimate inferred from Modesto's size and retail role (no published Turlock-specific leakage study exists), directionally certain but magnitude-unknown. Online/DTC and at-home substitution (grooming products, at-home gel/dip kits, clipper/DIY culture, at-home skincare) further cap per-visit and product-attach spend. The leakage and substitution magnitudes are the two largest acknowledged gaps in any operating-model plan and must travel as labeled unknowns.

pros.claim: Naming leakage and substitution as labeled unknowns keeps an operator from over-counting discretionary spend that drives to Modesto or stays home
pros.example: a premium spa concept discounting the destination spa-day demand that leaks north before committing capital

cons.claim: Because the magnitudes are unknown, the node can only bound the risk, not size it, limiting how far it informs a plan
cons.example: knowing leakage is real but unable to say what share of injectable demand Modesto captures

failure_modes: counting leaked discretionary spend as locally capturable
ignoring the at-home substitution cap on product-attach revenue
acceptance_tests: Modesto leakage and online/at-home substitution are stated as directionally-certain but magnitude-unknown labeled gaps affecting discretionary demand
revisit_triggers: a leakage study or local data becomes available
a Modesto entrant/exit or an at-home substitution trend shifts

base.update_signal: a leakage or at-home-substitution signal changes

nodes.definition: Model revenue, margin, and market-size honestly as labeled benchmark estimates and never as a named business's actual figures. Method: take a published industry benchmark (revenue per chair/station/provider/artist, or businesses-per-10k) times an observable size signal (chair/station/provider/artist count, format) with a sub-metro haircut, tag the result estimate-not-actual with method, public source, and a confidence level, and state the confirmation path. Two honesty flags travel always: the med-spa ~$1.4M-avg-per-location and the nail ~$34 revenue-per-capita are national benchmarks [ESTIMATE], never Turlock facts; and coverage is a floor, not a ceiling. Cash-heavy nail and tattoo likely understate true throughput, so those bands are conservative. No per-business dollar revenue is ever stated as fact.

included: the national-benchmark and floor-not-ceiling honesty flags

pros.claim: A labeled benchmark method gives a usable revenue/density estimate without ever asserting a private business's actuals
pros.example: estimating a barber's revenue as rev-per-chair x chair count, tagged medium-confidence with a benchmark source and a confirmation path

cons.claim: Benchmark estimates carry real uncertainty and mislead if the estimate-not-actual label is dropped downstream
cons.example: a med-spa national average quoted later as if it were a local fact

failure_modes: stating a per-business dollar figure as fact instead of a labeled estimate
quoting the med-spa national average or nail per-capita as a Turlock fact
acceptance_tests: every dollar/density figure is derived as benchmark x size signal, tagged estimate-not-actual with method, public source, and confidence, and the national-benchmark and floor caveats are carried
revisit_triggers: a published benchmark updates
actual invoice/receipt data becomes available to replace an estimate

base.update_signal: a published benchmark updates or actual data becomes available

nodes.definition: Harden the operating model against single-supplier failure by naming a backup source and a substitution rule for each critical input, so a stockout, price spike, or lost vendor does not halt service. Make the channel mix's partial redundancy explicit: a second nail wholesaler behind DTK/Beauty Zone, a backup barber-distributor, an alternate authorized medical distributor for injectables, a second tattoo-specialty source for sterile cartridges, and Amazon/direct-to-pro e-commerce as a fast gap-filler for fast-turn staples. For cold-chain injectables a backup must preserve the lot-tracked short-dated discipline, and for nail the W-2 cost shock makes a price/substitution response part of resilience. Redundancy is bought with a little cost against the larger cost of a service-stopping outage.

included: a backup source per critical input
the substitution rule and gap-fill path

pros.claim: A named backup per critical input turns a supplier outage from a service-stopping crisis into a routine substitution
pros.example: a nail salon switching to a second CA wholesaler the day its primary runs short of a core powder with no service gap

cons.claim: Maintaining backups across every input adds qualification effort and can split volume below each vendor's best price
cons.example: qualifying a second distributor used so rarely it never earns a volume break

failure_modes: single-sourcing the dominant input with no backup
naming a backup never actually qualified so it fails when called on
acceptance_tests: each critical input has a named backup source and a substitution rule, with cold-chain discipline preserved for injectables
revisit_triggers: a primary or backup supplier's availability changes
a price spike or shortage fires the substitution rule

base.update_signal: a primary or backup supplier's availability changes

nodes.definition: Assemble the consolidated operating-model plan that turns scattered decisions into one system: the sub-sector assignment, the licensing/establishment gate cleared, the per-format input profile, the supplier channel choice with a named primary and backup per input family, the capex anchor and labor model, the cold-chain/lot or sanitation/sterile compliance hooks, the labeled benchmark cost/revenue estimate per major line, and the cadence and resilience rules. It is the single artifact an operator works from to place first orders, set the chairs/stations/devices, hire under the right classification, and run weekly purchasing - with every dollar figure carried as a labeled estimate and coverage flagged as a floor.

excluded: individual node decisions already made upstream

pros.claim: One consolidated plan converts a pile of channel, capex, and labor decisions into an executable operating system with no orphaned input
pros.example: a single sheet listing every input, its primary and backup, channel, capex anchor, labor classification, and labeled cost estimate

cons.claim: A fixed plan can ossify and ignore a better mid-stream supplier or capex opportunity if not paired with a review loop
cons.example: sticking to one nail wholesaler when a second now beats it on a core SKU

failure_modes: a plan with an input that has no assigned supplier or backup
compliance hooks (cold chain, sterile, licensing) left off the plan
acceptance_tests: the plan lists every major input family with a primary, backup, channel, and cadence, plus the capex anchor, labor classification, compliance hooks, and labeled-cost estimate
revisit_triggers: a supplier, capex, labor, or compliance element of the plan changes
the review loop flags a better path

base.update_signal: a supplier, capex, labor, cadence, or compliance element of the plan changes

nodes.definition: Define the loop that keeps the operating-model plan alive: a fixed price-and-availability review cadence (e.g., a monthly distributor price-list check plus a quarterly full-mix and labor/compliance review) and the material-change triggers - a tracked input price spike, a lost or merged supplier, a worker-classification or licensing change (the live 2025 nail W-2 mandate is the model case), a med-spa device or injectable cost shift, a Modesto-leakage or demand signal change, a failed inspection, or a format/menu change - that send the operator back through SECTOR_SUBSECTOR_SPLIT and CHANNEL_MIX to re-plan. Without this loop the plan silently drifts out of cost, compliance, and resilience alignment.

included: re-entry into the sub-sector split and channel mix

pros.claim: A scheduled review catches price drift, a regulatory change, or supplier risk before it compresses a thin margin for months
pros.example: a quarterly review that catches the nail W-2 mandate's labor-cost impact and re-runs the pricing and labor plan

cons.claim: Reviewing too often churns suppliers and prevents any relationship or volume break from maturing
cons.example: re-tendering every input monthly so no distributor ever grants a loyalty price

failure_modes: no cadence set so the plan is never revisited and drifts
ignoring a material-change trigger and running a now-misaligned plan
acceptance_tests: a review cadence and an explicit list of material-change triggers exist, each routing back to SECTOR_SUBSECTOR_SPLIT and CHANNEL_MIX
revisit_triggers: a material-change trigger fires
the cadence proves too frequent or too sparse

base.update_signal: a material-change trigger fires or the cadence is tuned

the beauty-vs-medical split determines whether capex is thousands per station or six figures per device
the sub-sector sets whether the labor model is booth-rental, W-2, or medical delegation
the named-business roster grounds which suppliers are inferred or self-disclosed for each format
the cataloged floor count is the basis for the per-10k saturation read
individual licensure and the worker-classification rule gate which labor model is legal
medical-director oversight is the precondition for ordering prescription injectables
the body-art facility permit and Safe Body Art Act gate the tattoo supply setup
the medical-oversight requirement is half the med-spa entry wall
the channel-segmented supplier universe is the menu the channel choice selects from

the barber/hair channel choice sets up the distributor routing for those consumables
the nail channel choice sets up the CA wholesale ecosystem routing
the medical channel choice sets up the injectable distributor routing
the tattoo channel choice sets up the specialty-distributor routing

the capex band sets the buy-vs-lease decision for the capital anchor

the 2025 manicurist W-2 carve-out loss is the labor-cost half of the nail squeeze
the low-differentiation walk-in-substitutable nail format is the weak-pricing-power half of the squeeze
the in-town demand ceiling is trimmed by the leakage and substitution the leakage node sizes as unknown
the per-input cost profile feeds the benchmark x size-signal revenue estimate
the multi-channel mix is the partial redundancy the backup plan makes explicit
the single-sourced nail SKU long-tail needs a second wholesaler as backup
the short-dated injectable supply needs an alternate authorized medical distributor
the barber/hair sourcing is a core line of the consolidated plan
the capital anchor and smallwares stream are core lines of the plan
the labeled cost/revenue estimate per line is a required hook in the plan
the per-input backup and substitution rules are folded into the plan
the review loop watches the consolidated plan and triggers re-planning
a format or service-line change sends the operator back to re-assign the sub-sector
a price or supplier change re-runs the channel choice the plan depends on
mainstream salon distribution and the separate CA nail wholesale ecosystem compete for which channel an owner anchors on
edges.resolution_rule: route hair/barber color and clipper lines to CosmoProf/SalonCentric and barber-specialty distributors, but anchor the nail SKU long-tail on the DTK/ND/Beauty Zone nail ecosystem the mainstream channel does not stock

edges.why_related: buying capital outright competes with leasing or buying used for the same thin-margin cash
edges.resolution_rule: buy low-capex stations/chairs outright where cheap, but lease med-spa six-figure devices to clear the capital wall and preserve cash for consumables

edges.why_related: short-dated lot-tracked injectable procurement causally drives the cold-chain and FIFO discipline required to use it safely

conflict_axes.name: mainstream_distribution_vs_nail_ecosystem
conflict_axes.description: Anchoring on the mainstream CosmoProf/SalonCentric channel competes with the separate CA Vietnamese-American nail wholesale ecosystem that stocks the nail SKU long-tail.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: route color/barber lines to the mainstream channel and the nail SKU long-tail to DTK/ND/Beauty Zone

conflict_axes.name: beauty_distribution_vs_medical_procurement
conflict_axes.description: Low-capex consumables-light JIT beauty distribution and cold-chain lot-tracked medical procurement are structurally different supply disciplines for the same sector.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: assign the sub-sector first; never apply a beauty-JIT assumption to injectables or a medical-procurement burden to a barber

conflict_axes.name: booth_rental_vs_w2_employment
conflict_axes.description: Booth/chair rental converts owner revenue to rent and offloads COGS, but the 2025 mandate forces manicurists onto W-2 with higher effective labor cost.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use booth rental where the Borello carve-out still applies (hair/skin/barber); run nail as W-2 per the 2025 mandate

conflict_axes.name: buy_capital_vs_lease_devices
conflict_axes.description: Buying capital equipment outright competes with leasing or buying used for the same thin-margin cash, decisively so at the med-spa device tier.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: buy cheap low-capex stations; lease six-figure med-spa devices to clear the capital wall

conflict_axes.name: single_source_simplicity_vs_resilience
conflict_axes.description: Consolidating spend with one distributor simplifies ordering and earns volume breaks but concentrates outage and price risk on the dominant input.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: single-source non-critical consumables for the break; always keep a qualified backup for the dominant input

conflict_axes.name: authenticity_premium_vs_value_cost
conflict_axes.description: Premium brand inputs (named dip systems, multi-brand injectables, premium color) raise differentiation but cost more than commodity inputs a value-volume concept can recover.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: pay the premium where the clientele and ticket reward it; use commodity inputs for value-volume formats like walk-in nail/barber

conflict_axes.name: compliance_rigor_vs_throughput
conflict_axes.description: Strict cold-chain, lot, sanitation, and sterile-handling discipline protects safety and yield but adds labor that slows intake and throughput.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: apply the strictest checks to the highest-risk inputs (injectables, sterile tattoo supply) and streamline low-risk receiving

conflict_axes.name: local_capture_vs_modesto_leakage
conflict_axes.description: Building for locally-captured recurring-essential demand competes with chasing discretionary high-ticket demand that leaks north to Modesto.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: anchor on the captured recurring-essential spend; pursue discretionary headroom only with a leakage-aware convenience/trust edge

conflict_axes.name: benchmark_estimate_vs_stated_fact
conflict_axes.description: A labeled benchmark estimate disciplines planning but is weaker than a stated figure, tempting a drift to asserting revenue as fact about a named business.
poles: carry it as a labeled estimate
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: always carry revenue/margin/market-size as benchmark x size-signal estimates with method, source, and confidence; never assert a named-business actual

edge_cases.description: A nail salon keeps a booth-rental labor model after the 1/1/2025 manicurist W-2 mandate and incurs PAGA/misclassification exposure
edge_cases.trigger: a post-2025 nail operator treats manicurists as booth renters
edge_cases.mitigation: convert manicurists to W-2 per the 2025 mandate and budget the ~10-15%+ effective labor-cost step-up

edge_cases.description: A med spa orders prescription injectables with no physician medical-director of record or authorized-distributor account
edge_cases.trigger: a med-spa launch sources injectables outside the medical structure
edge_cases.mitigation: secure medical-director oversight and an authorized medical-distributor account before ordering any prescription product

edge_cases.description: A broken cold chain spoils a short-dated injectable lot before administration
edge_cases.trigger: a refrigeration gap in transport or storage on the most expensive input
edge_cases.mitigation: temperature-check every delivery, reject out-of-spec lots, rotate FIFO, and track lot numbers

edge_cases.description: A tattoo studio sources non-sterile needles or non-commercial inks in violation of the Safe Body Art Act
edge_cases.trigger: a body-art studio buys outside the single-use-sterile, commercial-ink mandate
edge_cases.mitigation: source only pre-sterilized single-use cartridges and commercial inks and run a steam autoclave for any reusables

edge_cases.description: The dominant input is single-sourced and the only distributor stocks out mid-week
edge_cases.trigger: the sole nail wholesaler or medical distributor runs short with no backup qualified
edge_cases.mitigation: pre-qualify a second source for every dominant input and switch on the substitution rule

edge_cases.description: A med-spa entrant under-capitalizes the six-figure device and medical-oversight wall
edge_cases.trigger: a white-space read treats med spa as easy-to-enter
edge_cases.mitigation: budget physician oversight and lease the device to clear the wall, reading the white-space as high-barrier-under-built

edge_cases.description: A new med spa over-orders short-dated injectables that expire before patient volume ramps
edge_cases.trigger: a launch order exceeds early booking demand
edge_cases.mitigation: match opening-order size to projected bookings and rotate FIFO with a top-up reorder cadence

edge_cases.description: An entrant adds an 8th nail salon or 6th barber into a locally saturated sub-category
edge_cases.trigger: a unit is added where adding only reshuffles share
edge_cases.mitigation: read the floor-not-ceiling saturation and pursue defensible headroom (med spa, event/cultural beauty) instead

edge_cases.description: A per-business revenue figure is stated as fact instead of a labeled benchmark estimate
edge_cases.trigger: a revenue or market-size number is quoted without the estimate-not-actual label
edge_cases.mitigation: derive every figure as benchmark x size signal, tag it estimate-not-actual with method/source/confidence and a confirmation path

edge_cases.description: A thin independents-only density ratio is misread as demand headroom
edge_cases.trigger: nail 0.97 vs ~3.4 national is cited as room to grow
edge_cases.mitigation: treat the ratio as a counting-method artifact (floor not ceiling) and read nail as locally crowded in lived terms

edge_cases.description: A nail SKU long-tail is over-stocked while fast-turn staples run short
edge_cases.trigger: working capital is tied up in slow-turn colors
edge_cases.mitigation: size the slow-turn long-tail to demand and keep fast-turn monomer/tips/files on a tight JIT reorder

workflow.action: Assign the format to a sub-sector
workflow.description: Place the format in the beauty-distribution or medical-procurement group and state the input/capex/labor implications
workflow.gate: the format is assigned with its input, capex, and labor implications

workflow.description: Enumerate the 25-business roster by sub-category with the floor caveat and confidence tiering
workflow.gate: the roster is enumerated with the floor-not-ceiling caveat

workflow.action: Clear the licensing and establishment gate
workflow.description: List BarberCosmo, medical-director, body-art, and City of Turlock requirements before any order
workflow.gate: the relevant licenses and (med-spa/body-art) special permits are documented before sourcing

workflow.description: Enumerate channel-segmented suppliers verified to serve the Central Valley and tag inference vs verified
workflow.gate: five+ channel segments each have a named geography-verified provider

workflow.action: Profile the dominant input cost center
workflow.description: Name the format's dominant consumable and rank the rest by spend and risk
workflow.gate: the dominant input is named and at least three more are ranked

workflow.description: Route each input family to the mainstream, nail-ecosystem, medical, or tattoo channel with rationale
workflow.gate: each input family is routed to a named channel with a rationale

workflow.description: Route barber/hair, nail, med-spa, tattoo, and spa inputs to named suppliers
workflow.gate: every menu input family is routed to a named or representative supplier

workflow.action: Set the capex anchor and labor model
workflow.description: Price the per-unit capex band, choose buy-vs-lease, and fix the labor classification
workflow.gate: the capex anchor and labor model are set, with nail flagged W-2 post-2025

workflow.description: Specify cold-chain/lot, sanitation, and sterile-handling controls per the risk profile
workflow.gate: the format's compliance and (med-spa) cold-chain controls are specified

workflow.action: Build labeled benchmark estimates and add backups
workflow.description: Derive revenue/cost as benchmark x size signal tagged estimate-not-actual, and name a backup per critical input
workflow.gate: every figure is labeled estimate-not-actual and each critical input has a named backup

workflow.action: Assemble the operating-model plan and review loop
workflow.description: Integrate suppliers, capex, labor, compliance, and cost hooks, then set the review cadence and triggers
workflow.gate: every major input has a primary, backup, channel, cadence, and compliance/cost hook with a review cadence set

dominance_rules.rule: Licensing and establishment readiness dominates any sourcing order
dominance_rules.rationale: no establishment can legally serve clients without its BarberCosmo license, no med spa without medical-director oversight, and no tattoo studio without a body-art permit
dominance_rules.trigger: any plan to place a first supplier order
dominance_rules.action: block sourcing until the format's licenses and special permits are in place

dominance_rules.rationale: running a post-2025 nail salon on booth rental violates the W-2 mandate and creates PAGA exposure that dwarfs the rent-model saving
dominance_rules.trigger: a nail labor model is set on a booth-rental basis
dominance_rules.action: classify manicurists as W-2 and budget the effective labor-cost step-up

dominance_rules.rule: Cold-chain and sterile integrity dominates cost optimization
dominance_rules.rationale: a broken cold chain on injectables or a non-sterile tattoo input spoils the costliest stock or creates liability that dwarfs any unit-price saving
dominance_rules.trigger: a sourcing choice trades cold-chain or sterile rigor for a lower price
dominance_rules.action: keep the compliance controls and find the saving elsewhere

dominance_rules.rule: Honesty labeling dominates any revenue or market-size figure
dominance_rules.rationale: a per-business dollar number stated as fact violates the financial-honesty charter and misleads planning
dominance_rules.trigger: any dollar or density figure about a named business or the sector
dominance_rules.action: express it only as a labeled benchmark estimate with method, source, and confidence

dominance_rules.rule: A backup for the dominant input dominates volume-discount consolidation
dominance_rules.rationale: an outage on the format's main input stops service, costing more than the consolidation discount earns
dominance_rules.trigger: the dominant input is about to be single-sourced
dominance_rules.action: qualify a second source before consolidating the rest

dominance_rules.rule: The sub-sector assignment dominates generic channel defaults
dominance_rules.rationale: the right channel, capex, and labor follow from the beauty-vs-medical split, not from a one-size salon default
dominance_rules.trigger: a sourcing decision made before the sub-sector is assigned
dominance_rules.action: assign the sub-sector first, then choose channels around it

dominance_rules.rule: Capital-wall realism dominates a naive med-spa white-space read
dominance_rules.rationale: reading med-spa headroom as easy-to-enter under-capitalizes the medical-oversight and six-figure-device wall
dominance_rules.trigger: a med-spa entry is planned on a demand-only basis
dominance_rules.action: budget physician oversight and device capital, reading the white-space as high-barrier-under-built

dominance_rules.rule: The review loop dominates impulse supplier switches
dominance_rules.rationale: structured review prevents churning a maturing distributor relationship over a transient price wiggle
dominance_rules.action: evaluate it through the review loop, not on impulse

dominance_rules.rule: Floor-not-ceiling reading dominates a literal per-10k saturation count
dominance_rules.rationale: the independents-only catalog excludes chains, counters, and solo operators, so a thin ratio is a counting artifact not headroom
dominance_rules.trigger: a per-10k density is read as room to grow
dominance_rules.action: treat the ratio as a floor and judge crowding in lived competitive terms

anti_rework_rules.rule: Clear the licensing and establishment gate before placing any supplier order
anti_rework_rules.prevents: buying inventory or devices an establishment cannot yet legally use to serve clients

anti_rework_rules.rule: Assign the sub-sector before choosing channels, capex, and labor
anti_rework_rules.prevents: building a beauty-JIT plan around a medical format or vice versa and re-doing it later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Qualify a backup for every critical input before single-sourcing it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a service-stopping outage with no substitute ready when the primary fails

anti_rework_rules.rule: Verify a supplier actually serves the Central Valley before building it into the plan
anti_rework_rules.prevents: designing a plan around a vendor whose minimums or reach exclude the region

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set cold-chain receiving and lot control before the first injectable delivery
anti_rework_rules.prevents: spoiling high-cost short-dated injectables on day one for lack of a receiving standard

anti_rework_rules.rule: Classify nail labor as W-2 from the start under the 2025 mandate
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a booth-rental misclassification and retroactive PAGA/workers'-comp exposure

anti_rework_rules.rule: Label every revenue and market-size figure estimate-not-actual when first written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a planning estimate being quoted downstream as a measured per-business fact

anti_rework_rules.rule: Read every per-10k density as a floor when first computed
anti_rework_rules.prevents: misreading a counting-method artifact as demand headroom and over-building a saturated sub-category

anti_rework_rules.rule: Budget the med-spa device and oversight wall before assuming the white-space
anti_rework_rules.prevents: under-capitalizing a med-spa entry and stalling at launch

iteration_protocol.trigger: the operator changes or adds a format or service line
iteration_protocol.action: re-assign the sub-sector and re-run the input profile, channel mix, and plan

iteration_protocol.trigger: a worker-classification or licensing rule changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-clear the licensing gate and re-fix the labor model and nail-squeeze response

iteration_protocol.trigger: a primary supplier is lost, merges, or stocks out
iteration_protocol.action: activate the backup, re-qualify the channel, and update the plan

iteration_protocol.trigger: a tracked input price spikes or a med-spa device/injectable cost shifts
iteration_protocol.action: trigger substitution or a lease/buy re-evaluation and re-run the cost estimate

iteration_protocol.trigger: a cold-chain, sanitation, or body-art compliance requirement changes or an inspection fails
iteration_protocol.action: re-specify the compliance and receiving controls

iteration_protocol.trigger: a demographic, CSU-enrollment, or density-benchmark input changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the demand-ceiling saturation read and the labeled revenue estimate

iteration_protocol.trigger: a Modesto-leakage or at-home-substitution signal changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-bound the discretionary-demand gap and the med-spa/premium-spa headroom read

iteration_protocol.trigger: the review cadence proves too frequent or too sparse
iteration_protocol.action: tune the review loop cadence and trigger list

priority_rationale: Foundational sub-sector assignment, named-business grounding, the licensing gate, and supplier-universe mapping precede channel and format sourcing because every choice depends on the beauty-vs-medical split, the real roster, the legal preconditions, and the verified vendor set; the channel and format-sourcing nodes plus capex and labor build the operating mix; the nail W-2 squeeze, med-spa barrier, demand-ceiling, leakage, cold-chain, resilience, and honesty nodes compose those into a hardened, honestly-costed system; and the consolidated plan and review loop come last because they assemble and then watch the whole plan, routing material changes back to the foundations.
